name: Convert documented current-account income and wire USD to your U.S. account
legality: Lawful when the funds and documents qualify
pros: Cheapest lawful route: one spread, one wire, one cable. No annual amount limit if the bank accepts the source documents.
cons: The bank must accept that the CNY is a lawful, documented current-account item (salary, pension, sale of a personal item, etc.). Accumulated savings with no traceable source may be refused.
requires: Passport/ID, source-of-funds documents, Chinese tax records where the bank asks; a written checklist from the branch before you convert.
verdict: The default recommendation if you can document where the money came from.

name: Use the USD 50,000 annual convenience amount, year after year
legality: Lawful for 境内个人; not a way to move USD 400,000 quickly
pros: No source documents beyond your ID for each USD 50,000 slice. The threshold is not an annual cap, so larger documented items can still be taken to the bank.
cons: USD 400,000 is eight calendar years and eight wires, each with its own cable fee. Borrowing a relative's quota is expressly penalised.
requires: Chinese ID/passport treated as 境内个人 (Chinese citizen, or a foreigner resident in China for 1+ continuous year).
verdict: Fallback only: lawful, but slow and not cheaper than W1.

name: Emigrant property transfer (移民财产转移) after SAFE approval
pros: Covers the whole estate, no amount ceiling, and since 2014 one approval can be paid out in one or several remittances.
cons: Requires cancelled mainland hukou, a consular certificate of settlement abroad, and PRC tax clearance. Only available to someone who has actually emigrated and cancelled registration.
requires: 户籍注销证明, 中国使领馆出具的定居证明, 税收证明/完税凭证, property-right documents; approval by the FX bureau at the former hukou location.
verdict: Best route if — and only if — you have emigrated and cancelled your hukou.

name: Inheritance transfer (继承财产转移)
pros: No amount ceiling; approval sits with the FX bureau at the deceased's former hukou location; several inheritances can be combined in one application since 2014.
cons: Death certificate, notarised inheritance documents, PRC tax clearance; grants of probate abroad may need translation and authentication.
requires: Inheritance documents, death certificate, identity documents, tax clearance.
verdict: The route for inherited money, not for your own savings.

name: Remit the proceeds of selling mainland residential property
legality: Lawful when documented; the PRC 20% tax on the gain is the real cost
pros: Sale proceeds of a self-used home can be converted and remitted with the sale contract and tax records.
cons: PRC IIT at 20% of the gain (with possible exemptions for a main home) dwarfs the FX cost; the tax depends on cost basis and holding period, which this model cannot know.
requires: Sale contract, property certificate, PRC tax clearance, self-use evidence.
verdict: Route is cheap; the tax on the gain is not (blank here — fact-dependent).

name: Re-convert unused RMB against the original exchange memo (原兑换未用完人民币兑回)
pros: No convenience-amount question at all if the original inbound exchange is evidenced.
cons: Capped at the amount you originally brought in, and the memo is only good for 24 months.
requires: Original exchange memo (水单), ID, within 24 months.
verdict: Free of the quota problem, but only if you personally brought the FX in.

name: Wire out foreign currency already sitting in your Chinese FX account
legality: Lawful when the account and remittance are accepted
pros: No CNY→USD spread at all: the only cost is the wire and cable fee.
cons: Only works for the part of the balance that is already USD (or another hard currency). The bank still reviews the remittance.
requires: FX savings-account balance and ID: Art. 15(1) of the implementation rules requires only the ID for a 境外个人 remitting from an FX savings account.
verdict: Always check this first: any USD already in the account should move before any CNY is converted.

name: PRC company dividend / profit distribution to the U.S. owner
legality: Lawful when the company and tax documents qualify
pros: A formal capital-account route for company money; a tax treaty may reduce PRC withholding.
cons: Company profit tax, 20% PRC dividend IIT (statutory) less any treaty relief, audit and tax-recordal work. Not a personal-savings shortcut.
requires: Board resolution, audited accounts, tax-recordal form, dividend withholding payment.
verdict: Only if the money is genuinely company money you own.

name: Withdraw cash abroad on a Chinese UnionPay debit card
legality: Lawful but capped far below USD 400,000
pros: No bank visit, no source documents; immediate USD cash.
cons: About 1.12% in BOC fees plus an unpublished card-network spread; USD 400,000 would take about 27 calendar years under the RMB 100,000 annual ceiling, and exceeding that ceiling suspends overseas cash withdrawal for the rest of the year and the whole next year.
requires: UnionPay debit card, overseas ATM, travel not required if the card is used abroad by you.
verdict: Expensive and slow; not a route for a large balance.

name: Withdraw cash abroad on a Chinese Visa / Mastercard debit card
legality: Lawful but capped far below USD 400,000
pros: 2.5% is published and predictable; no bank visit.
cons: 2.5% is roughly twelve times the bank spread, the same RMB 100,000 annual ceiling applies, and breaching it suspends overseas cash withdrawal for this year and the next.
requires: Visa/Mastercard debit card issued in China.
verdict: The most expensive lawful cash route in this table.

name: Buy USD cash and carry it out by hand
legality: Lawful only within the cash-control rules
pros: No wire fee and no cable fee; only the spread. Useful for a few thousand dollars.
cons: USD 10,000 per trip at most (permit above USD 5,000), 40 trips for USD 400,000, physical-loss and seizure risk, and FinCEN Form 105 on the U.S. side.
requires: 携带证 from a designated bank for USD 5,000–10,000; FinCEN Form 105 above USD 10,000 on arrival.
verdict: Cheap per dollar, impractical per year, and the most heavily policed route.

name: Move RMB to Hong Kong and convert at the offshore CNH rate
legality: Conditional — no general personal channel documented
pros: Offshore CNH pricing can be tighter than onshore retail in some periods.
cons: A personal cross-border RMB remittance needs the same current-account evidence; no official source publishes a personal CNH retail tariff, so the cost is blank.
requires: A lawful reason to remit RMB offshore plus a Hong Kong account; eligibility must be confirmed in writing.
verdict: Not priced here — no official tariff exists to cite.

name: Use a licensed payment institution / fintech outward service
legality: Conditional — depends on the provider's licence and your purpose
pros: Potentially convenient if a licensed provider accepts your purpose and corridor.
cons: No regulator publishes the provider's corridor price, spread or eligibility for this case; quotes must be obtained individually.
verdict: Unpriced: obtain a written quote and compare with W1.

name: Split the balance across relatives' USD 50,000 quotas
cons: Borrowing another person's convenience amount puts you on the watch list for this year and the next two, and the conduct can be penalised under the FX Regulations at up to 30% of the amount (30%–100% if serious).

name: Underground bank / matched orders (地下钱庄, 对敲)
cons: Art. 45: warning, confiscation of gains, fine up to 30% (30%–100% if serious), criminal referral.

name: Buy USDT or another stablecoin in China and sell it abroad
cons: Virtual-currency business activity is illegal financial activity in China; the 2026 notice keeps the prohibition and extends it to offshore exchanges serving mainland residents.

name: Leave the money in CNY, or spend it abroad on a UnionPay card
pros: Zero conversion cost today; card spending does not consume the convenience amount.
cons: Delivers goods, not USD. The FX, tax and reporting questions simply move to your estate or to a later date.
